segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The elder, to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Beloved, I pray that in every respect it may go well with you and that you may be in good health, just as it goes well with your soul.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I rejoiced greatly when brothers came and testified to your truth, to how you are walking in truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I have no greater joy than this, to hear that my children are walking in the truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Beloved, you act faithfully in whatever you do for the brothers, strangers though they are.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They have testified to your love before the assembly. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they set out for the sake of the Name, taking nothing from the pagans.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So we ought to take such people in, so that we may become co-workers with the truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I wrote something to the assembly, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, does not receive us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason, if I come, I will bring up the things he is doing, spouting malicious nonsense about us. And not content with that, he does not receive the brothers himself, and those who want to he stops and throws out of the assembly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Beloved, do not imitate what is evil but what is good. The one who does good is from God; the one who does evil has not seen God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Everyone testifies in Demetrius’s favor, and so does the truth itself. We testify too, and you know that our testimony is true.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I had many things to write to you, but I do not want to write to you with ink and pen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I hope to see you soon, and we will speak face to face.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peace to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends by name.

notes.note: The verb can mean either 'pray' or simply 'wish'. A wish for the recipient's health was a standard opening in Greek letters of the period, so a first-century reader would hear a familiar courtesy here, given a Christian turn by the reference to the soul. The verse is a conventional greeting, not a promise of prosperity.

The Greek word meant a gathering of people: a city's citizen assembly, or in the Greek Old Testament Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses 'assembly' throughout so that the reader sees one word for one Greek word, though it can sound like a one-off meeting.

notes.traditional: send them on their journey / bring forward on their journey
notes.note: In early Christian usage this verb was close to a technical term for equipping travellers for the next stage of a journey with food, money and sometimes companions. Gaius is being asked for practical support, not merely a farewell.

notes.traditional: his name's sake / the sake of the Name
notes.note: The Greek says only 'the name' without saying whose. Most interpreters take it as the name of Jesus, as elsewhere in early Christian speech about missionaries; others hear the Jewish reverential use of 'the Name' for God. The Greek does not decide between them.

The word means 'people of the nations', that is, those outside God's people. Many versions translate 'Gentiles', but Gaius and his circle bear Greek names and were probably non-Jews themselves, so the contrast is with unbelievers, not with an ethnic group. The point is that the travelling brothers did not take support from those they were evangelising. Some versions accordingly have 'pagans' or 'non-believers'.

The Greek can mean working together with the truth, the truth being pictured as itself active (as in verse 12, where it testifies), or working together with the missionaries for the truth. Translations and commentators are divided, and either reading fits the context.

notes.traditional: receiveth us not / does not acknowledge our authority
notes.note: The same verb is used in verse 10 for refusing hospitality to the travelling brothers, and it is rendered the same way in both places. Here it may mean that Diotrephes refuses to welcome the elder's emissaries, or more broadly that he does not accept the elder's authority; many versions choose the second. 'Us' may refer to the elder alone or to him and his associates.

notes.traditional: Demetrius hath good report of all men
notes.note: This verse follows the form of an ancient letter of recommendation. Demetrius was probably the bearer of the letter and one of the travelling brothers whom Gaius is being asked to welcome, though the letter does not say so explicitly.

The Greek is literally 'mouth to mouth', a Semitic idiom found in the Greek Old Testament for direct personal speech. 'Face to face' is the English equivalent; the literal phrase would mislead a modern reader.

Verse numbering differs between editions here. Some English Bibles, including the King James Version, print these closing greetings as the end of verse 14 and have no verse 15. The wording is not affected.

candidates.reason: It occurs in Matthew and here with the sense 'outsider to God's people', and translations vary between 'Gentiles', 'pagans' and 'unbelievers'; it also needs distinguishing from ἔθνη.
It is frequent in the letters as an address, where versions split between 'beloved' and 'dear friend(s)', and the link to ἀγαπάω and ἀγάπη is lost if the English varies.
The plural is used throughout the New Testament for fellow believers, and a single policy is needed on 'brothers' versus 'brothers and sisters'.
It is a near-technical term for materially equipping travellers in Acts, Paul and Titus, and should be rendered consistently so that the practice is recognisable.
The verb and its noun are thematic in the Johannine writings and recur across the New Testament, and alternating 'testify', 'bear witness' and 'speak well of' hides the repetition.
